title: the sounds
hook: a fingertip on the side of the nose, a hum, and the dot that writes it down
tomorrow: someone reads your name off a list wrong. does it really matter?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sounds and two old answers on saying them right: the chanter's care and the devotee's heart, both inside the tradition. Today, a sound that lives partly in the nose.

Singers warm up before a show with their mouths closed. A kid hums under her breath before a test, and a grandmother hums over the stove. A lot of steadying starts with a hum. Try it now: rest one fingertip on the side of the nose and hum, softly. It buzzes. The sound isn't only in the mouth anymore; it's in the nose, and somewhere behind the eyes. Sanskrit has a mark for exactly that buzz. A single dot.
screen: `A HUM BEFORE THE SHOW.` → `A FINGERTIP ON THE NOSE.` → `IT BUZZES.`

segments.voice: Panini defines it in one line: a sound made with the mouth and the nose together is anunasika, nasal. The dot written above a letter is the anusvara, the after-sound. Look at the word Sanskrit itself, in Devanagari: संस्कृत. There's the dot, over the very first letter. Sam. Here's the useful part. The dot doesn't have one fixed sound. It's a hum that takes the shape of whatever comes next. Before a k, it hums at the back of the mouth, as ng: Shankara, said SHUNG-kuh-ruh. Before a t at the teeth, it becomes an n. Before a b or a p at the lips, an m. And before an s, where nothing closes, it stays a pure buzz in the nose, the very hum you just felt. One dot, many shapes, each decided by the neighbor. The hum at the end of Om has its own mark too: a little moon with a dot in it, the chandrabindu, telling the voice to let the sound ring through the nose. So a singer's warm-up and the close of Om are made in the same place. Today's sound isn't only heard. It's felt in the bones of the face.
screen: `MOUTH AND NOSE TOGETHER.` · `THE DOT: THE AFTER-SOUND.` · `IT TAKES THE NEXT LETTER'S SHAPE.` · `A MOON AND A DOT ON OM.` · then, large: `FELT AS MUCH AS HEARD.`

segments.voice: Close the lips and hum softly on each out-breath, one fingertip resting on the side of the nose to feel the buzz. Let each hum last as long as the breath likes, no longer. Then let the hum stop, and feel how the quiet sits in the face.
The sounds: today, the hum. One dot, the anusvara, that borrows its shape from the letter after it.
Your line: the sounds. Some of them are felt as much as heard, right in the bones of the face. Day done.

howItsDone: In Devanagari the anusvara is written as a dot above the letter and the chandrabindu as a moon with a dot; chanters let Om close on a long, humming m.

chat.meaning: The anusvara is a hum shaped by the next letter. Before b, made at the lips, it comes out as m.

anusvara.meaning: the dot above a letter: a hum shaped by the next sound

anunasika.meaning: a sound made with the mouth and the nose together

Shankara.meaning: a name of Shiva, the kind one

chandrabindu.meaning: a moon with a dot: the sound rings through the nose

Om.meaning: the sacred syllable, closing on a hum

sources.ref: Ashtadhyayi 1.1.8 (mukhanasikavacano 'nunasikah: a sound uttered with mouth and nose is nasal)
Ashtadhyayi 8.4.58 (anusvarasya yayi parasavarnah: before a stop, the anusvara takes the nasal of the following sound)
Devanagari: anusvara (dot) and chandrabindu (moon and dot); संस्कृत, शंकर, ॐ

notes: 2026-10-14 v3 rewrite (recipe v3, shape senses): new lesson recipe data (chat, gloss, recall) included; confirm the chat reply, glosses, scripts and pronunciations with the Keeper.
Written fresh in v3. The practice is physical (humming, fingertip on the nose) and fits the breathing timer.
Anusvara before a stop becomes the homorganic nasal (8.4.58; obligatory within a word, optional across words); before sibilants it stays a nasal glide. Confirm the plain-English description.
Chandrabindu on ॐ: the common glyph of Om carries the chandrabindu. Confirm phrasing ('a little moon with a dot').
Gloss 'Shankara: a name of Shiva, the kind one' (śaṃ-kara, maker of welfare/auspiciousness): confirm 'the kind one' or prefer 'the one who brings good'.
Priya picks up her line here: vasudhaiva kutumbakam (कुटुम्बकम्, often written कुटुंबकम् with the anusvara before b). Its meaning and sandhi are taught on day 1455.
